facts.claim: A Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, because local authorities may ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices across Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: The brief's old URL /consular-services/notarial-services/cni redirects here; cite the canonical URL.

facts.claim: At least one person applying for the CNI must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. Supporting documents: Australian citizen, a valid Australian passport; permanent resident, a valid foreign passport with evidence of permanent residence; foreign citizen partner, a valid foreign passport or photo ID; divorced, a Divorce Certificate; widowed, the deceased partner's Death Certificate; under 18, a judicial authorisation from an Australian court. Originals or certified true copies; non-English documents need a professional English translation.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI: download and complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants the CNI or other documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay the fee on submission. Incomplete applications are not processed (mailed ones are returned with a letter). Collect from the Passport Office or mission, or receive it by registered post in a self-addressed envelope you supply.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Step list. DFAT may contact the issuer of supporting documents to check authenticity, which 'could cause a delay'. No processing time is published on this page; see needs.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars, for services in Australia and overseas: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105; Authentication certificate AUD 105. In Australia payment is by EFTPOS, MasterCard or Visa only; cash is not accepted. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.use_note: Write as 'AUD 181 per CNI (DFAT fee for 2026)' and 'AUD 105 per apostille'. A wedding in 2027 will be at the 2027 CPI-indexed fee: say 'fees rise each 1 January'. The fee table is per CNI; whether each partner needs their own CNI: the Australian Embassy Athens says a CNI is required 'for each non-Greek citizen' (F-105), so two Australians should budget two CNIs (inference, confirm).

facts.claim: DFAT advises couples to confirm before applying: whether a CNI is needed at all (some authorities accept a Single Status Certificate or No Record Result Certificate from a state or territory births, deaths and marriages registry); whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage (if so, the Australian embassy there can issue it); whether it needs an apostille or authentication certificate; and what other documents are required, such as a birth certificate, divorce certificate or deceased partner's death certificate, which come from the BDM registry or the issuing court. Some foreign governments also ask for the original or a copy of the CNI application form, which DFAT can provide. DFAT cannot advise on another country's legal process.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Supports the 'confirm with your municipality' house rule.

facts.claim: The Australian Embassy in Athens says a CNI is required by both religious and municipal organisations in Greece for each non-Greek citizen wishing to marry there. The acceptable place of issue (the Embassy in Greece, a DFAT office in Australia, or another Australian mission) can differ significantly between organisations, so couples should first confirm documents and place of issue with the priest or celebrant, or their wedding planner. The application may be lodged with the Embassy in Athens or at any DFAT office in Australia for issue in Greece. The CNI is issued in English.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Greece, Getting married in Greece
facts.use_note: Page is undated and links to old smartraveller.gov.au/guide/ URLs, so it is old; medium. 'Lodged... in Australia for issue in Greece' suggests a CNI issued by the Embassy can be applied for from Australia; Wedded Advisor to confirm current practice with the Embassy.

facts.claim: The Australian Embassy in Athens says most Greek organisations require all documents (CNI, birth, baptismal, divorce or death certificates) translated into Greek, and that it is practice in Greece to accept only official translations by the Greek Ministry of Foreign Affairs Translation Section in Athens or a Greek consulate or embassy abroad, which charge for the service.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Greece, Getting married in Greece
facts.use_note: CONFLICT flagged in the brief: the Greek Ministry of Interior's 2021 circulars describe abolition of the MFA translation service and a new official translation system. Batch A (Greek side) must resolve; do not state the MFA-only rule as current.

facts.claim: DFAT legalises Australian public documents with an apostille applied directly to the document (or to a notarised copy if you do not want the original marked, provided the overseas authority accepts it). Documents that are not original Australian public documents must first be notarised by an Australian Notary Public. Request with a Document Legalisation Request Form signed in front of an authorised witness, then submit by appointment at any Australian Passport Office (Adelaide, Brisbane, Canberra, Darwin, Hobart, Melbourne, Perth, Sydney; someone can attend on your behalf), at an Australian embassy or consulate overseas, or by registered post to the Australian Passport Office Authentications Section in Melbourne or Sydney with a self-addressed registered return envelope and credit card authorisation. Several documents can go on one form and one appointment.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised
facts.use_note: Apostille row of the documents table. Fee in F-103. Greece and Australia are both Hague Apostille Convention parties (Greece side to be confirmed by batch A if cited).

facts.claim: DFAT does not publish a fixed processing time for legalisation: 'Processing times vary', with delays at the end of the school year and during peak holiday periods, when a request is incomplete or unpaid, or when DFAT must contact the document's issuing authority.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised
facts.use_note: No official CNI or apostille turnaround exists; the article must not give a number of days. Point out that the December to January peak is a slow period, relevant to couples applying over summer for a European-summer wedding.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry. Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm an overseas certificate is valid in Australia.
facts.use_note: Core answer for the paying parent. Do not add legal advice beyond this wording.

facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name; check your state or territory BDM registry. Australian rules referenced: not married, not marrying a close relative, at least 18 (or 16 to 18 with court approval), free and informed consent. The right to marry in Australia is no longer determined by sex or gender.
facts.use_note: Second official source for recognition, consistent with F-109. Legal basis is the Marriage Act 1961 (Part VA, recognition of foreign marriages) linked from both pages at https://www.legislation.gov.au/Series/C1961A00012 ; section text not read in this batch, so cite Part VA by name only. Same-sex marriages valid in Greece (Law 5089/2024 per brief) therefore fall within the general rule; one line only.

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: if you change your family name because of marriage you may keep using your current passport or get a new one (book travel in the name in your passport). For a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent (born overseas, live overseas, or married overseas, having become a citizen before the marriage), must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service. For a replacement-passport fee waiver, a foreign marriage certificate is accepted without legalisation but still needs a full approved translation.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: KEY POINT for the writer: an Australian-born spouse who marries in Greece cannot put the Greek certificate straight into a new passport; they first register a change of name with their state BDM. Page last-modified header 11 Nov 2026. Translation services page: https://www.passports.gov.au/help/interpreting-and-translation (not read).

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages change of name policy: a person legally married in Australia can take their spouse's family name without registering an official change of name. The exemption is worded for marriages in Australia. To register a change of name in NSW, the person's birth must be registered in NSW, or they must have been born overseas and lived in NSW for three consecutive years, or a court must order it. Adults apply with proof of identity, a reason, criminal record disclosure, consent to a National Police Check and the fee. Limits: one change in 12 months and three in a lifetime. Documents not in English must be translated by an accredited translator, such as a NAATI translator.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Change of name policy
facts.use_note: Medium because the policy does not say in so many words what happens after an overseas marriage; read together with F-111 (Passport Office needs an RBDM name change certificate for an Australian-born person married overseas) and F-110 (some states do not accept overseas certificates for name change). Article line: 'If you were born in Australia and want your married name in your passport, expect to register a change of name with your state or territory registry, using the Greek certificate with a NAATI translation. Check your own state's rules.' Fee not read: see needs. NSW only; other states not checked.

facts.claim: The NSW Registry requires foreign documents not in English to be translated in full and stamped by a NAATI-accredited translator, with copies of both the original and the translation. Where a name on an identity document differs from the application, a linking document such as a marriage certificate is needed; for events outside NSW a copy of the certificate must be supplied.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, Proving your identity for NSW Registry applications
facts.use_note: Translation for use at home: NAATI (Australia) for the Greek certificate, which is the opposite direction to the Greek-side translation question. Do not imply NAATI translations are accepted in Greece.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's Greece advice (still current at 13 November 2026, level: exercise normal safety precautions) says Greece is in the Schengen area; Australians can enter for a short stay (90 days or less) without a visa in some cases, must register biometric details (fingerprints and photo) under the EU Entry/Exit System (EES) on arrival, and should check EES and visa rules before travel. ETIAS is not yet operating: the EU will announce its launch date several months ahead, after which visa-free travellers to participating countries will need an ETIAS travel authorisation before travel, applied for only through the official EU website.
facts.use_note: For the FAQ 'How long can Australians stay in Greece?'. Medium because the page was read via text extraction and the full 90-in-180-days wording sits on the linked Schengen page (https://www.smartraveller.gov.au/before-you-go/basics/visas-and-entry-requirements-europe-and-schengen-area), not read. 'Still current at' date is Smartraveller's own (Australian time). Write: '90 days or less for a short stay, per Smartraveller; check the Schengen rules and ETIAS status before you book.'

legal.summary: CNI AUD 181, apostille AUD 105 each (DFAT, 2026 fees, CPI-indexed each 1 January). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
CNI required for each non-Greek party by municipal and religious bodies; acceptable place of issue varies by organisation. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in Greece and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
Passport in married name: Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Wedded Advisor confirms the current process.
